When a round price becomes a tax line

At exactly $2 million, the number of recorded sales relative to nearby price density falls from 7.8 to 1.6 across the 2019 reform.

This compares different periods using a local-density ratio. It is evidence of transaction shifting around the threshold; it does not identify who ultimately bears the tax.

The cash gap changes with the transfer screen

In repeat sales of houses, the financed-minus-cash contrast falls from 9.25 to 4.87 log points after excluding deeds with shared buyer and seller surnames.

Shared surnames are a proxy for possible related transfers. The comparison does not identify the causal effect of cash financing. The current paper reports additional financing-review sensitivities.

A recorded amount can shift a price index

Removing deeds flagged as legal-rule transfers changes the repeat-sales index path. The largest gap is 3.7 log points in 2010 Q3.

Neither path is a verified true-price index. Uncertainty is conditional on the labels and matching rules. The difference in the total peak-to-trough decline is small and its interval includes zero.

The graphics pack contains eight graphics as PNG and SVG, CSV data and source notes. The interactive explorer adds filtered chart downloads. Its recorded-price medians describe the mix of transactions; they are not estimates of price appreciation.

A data story worth checking

Condominium deed-linkage coverage differs by borough and recorded price. A comparison based only on successfully linked units can select a different slice of the market. Read the coverage story or compare the aggregates.

Research and provenance

The papers use public Department of Finance sales files and ACRIS deeds and mortgages. Each paper page links to its current PDF and fixed replication archive. These are observational measurement studies with different samples. The companion simulation is illustrative. The property-record guide explains the distinctions behind the headlines.
